The napkin holds. Every fork found 99.6% of its prompt in the cache, which is all of it except the instruction. Eight forks of a 63K context added 2.6K tokens to the peak, not 8 × 63K. And the parent did not notice: its next turn waited 0.31 s with no forks and 0.31 s with eight.
The costs show up elsewhere. On Qwen3-8B the decode step grew from 23 to 29 ms with 8 forks, because each fork reads the parent’s whole context on every step: the cache is shared, the reading is not. That is R3 again. On Qwen3.5 the step barely moved, since most of its layers read a fixed-size state instead of the context. What Qwen3.5 pays instead is state slots, 5 per running fork. The peak went from 16 slots to 44, 44K tokens’ worth of memory for 8 forks, against 3.0K tokens of cache. On the hybrid model, a fork’s memory goes almost entirely into state.






Command: sessions, priorities and forks





Sessions, with the cache kept for open sessions (--enable-session-radix-cache at launch):
import requests
URL = "http://localhost:30000"

sid = requests.post(URL + "/open_session", json={"capacity_of_str_len": 1 << 30, "timeout": 120}).json()

def turn(rid, ids, prev_rid=None, offset=None):
    sp = {"id": sid} | ({"rid": prev_rid, "offset": offset} if prev_rid else {})
    r = requests.post(URL + "/generate", json={"rid": rid, "input_ids": ids, "session_params": sp,
                      "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 300, "temperature": 0, "ignore_eos": True}}).json()
    if r["meta_info"]["finish_reason"]["type"] == "abort":   # the session expired while this request ran
        raise RuntimeError(r["meta_info"]["finish_reason"])
    return r

turn("t0", system + task)                                    # each later turn sends only its new tokens,
turn("t1", tool_result, prev_rid="t0", offset=len(system + task))  # spliced in after `offset` tokens of t0
requests.post(URL + "/close_session", json={"session_id": sid})
Priorities (--radix-eviction-policy priority): add "priority": 1 to the /generate body for a turn whose tool call will come back soon, 0 otherwise.
A fork is nothing special: send the parent’s prompt plus the sub-agent’s instruction as a new request, and the radix tree finds the shared prefix by itself.





Where this leaves me
Choosing who stays does not help, because past the cliff there is almost nothing left to choose. The memory belongs to the requests that are running, and each of them holds a whole 72K context for about a minute while it decodes (Chapter 2). Below the cliff, LRU is already about right for real tool waits. Two findings are worth keeping anyway, and both are operational. SGLang never preempts a running request, so overload is a queue. And its session timeout counts from a request’s arrival, so a timeout shorter than a slow turn throws the session away.
So the lever is the size of what each running request holds. The next chapters make it smaller.

title: Keeping 32 agents warm on one GPU
text:
Chapter 4: Holding it once
Chapter 3 ended on a single lever: the size of what each agent holds. The cheapest way to make it smaller is to not hold anything twice.
The radix tree already does this for one thing. The synthetic agents all start with the same 35K-token system prompt, the tree stores it once (Figure 12), and Chapter 2’s napkin counted it once:
\[
\text{pool} = S + N \cdot (c - S)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
N_\text{max} = \frac{\text{pool} - S}{c - S}
\]
with \(S\) the shared prefix and \(c\) the context each agent holds. Two questions follow. Is there more than the system prompt to share? And what does sharing cost when the agents belong to different customers?

Is there more to share?
A prefix match stops at the first token that differs. After that, nothing is reused, even text the server has seen before. That is not SGLang being lazy. Chapter 0 showed that a token’s key and value depend on every token before it: through attention, and through RoPE on its position. So a file the agent reads at turn 3 and again at turn 9 gets different keys and values the second time, because everything in front of it is different.
Methods like CacheBlend (Yao et al., 2024) reuse such chunks anyway. They take the cached keys and values of the repeated text, then recompute a small fraction of its tokens to patch up the attention to what now comes before them. It is an approximation, and before reaching for one it is worth counting what it could find.
The AgentX trace fingerprints every 64-token block, so I walked each session in order. For every request I counted the blocks covered by a prefix some earlier request of the session had already sent, and, among the rest, the blocks that had appeared anywhere earlier in the session.
Of 3,248,228 blocks, 94.4% are prefix hits. Outside a prefix, 0 repeat. Not few: none. These agents never re-send content out of order; they append. A non-prefix cache would have nothing to do here.
Two limits on that zero. The fingerprints are local to each session, so a file two different sessions both read is invisible. And a block only matches if the same 64 tokens start on a block boundary, so the same text at a different offset counts as new. Neither changes the picture inside a session, which is where an agent’s context comes from.


What the shared prompt is worth
So the sharing that exists is the prefix. To see what it is worth, I made it optional. In the synthetic workload, each agent starts either with the shared system prompt or with a private prompt of the same length, which the tree has to store separately. If a fraction \(f\) of the agents share it, the shared copy is stored once and every other agent carries its own:
\[
N_\text{max}(f) = \frac{\text{pool} - f\,S}{(c - S) + (1 - f)\,S}
\]
I ran 24 agents on Qwen3-8B with \(f\) = 0, ½ and 1.

Sharing the system prompt halves what each agent holds, and that roughly doubles the agents that fit, from 6.9 to 13.2. 24 agents is past the cliff in every row, so the hit rate is Chapter 2’s floor: the only thing that survives is the shared prompt. With nobody sharing, there is no floor, and the hit rate is zero. With everybody sharing it is 59%, and the median wait drops from 186 s to 42 s.
A system prompt is free compression of the cache, on one condition: every agent has to send exactly the same one, byte for byte. That is Chapter 1’s lesson again, at the scale of the whole server instead of one session.


What sharing leaks
Now let the agents belong to different customers. R6 says one customer must learn nothing about another, and a shared cache is a side channel. A prompt someone else already sent skips its prefill, so it comes back faster, and the speed is visible to whoever sent it second.
How much faster is a matter of arithmetic. Prefilling 4,096 tokens on Qwen3-8B costs about 166 ms on the napkin, and a full hit costs one step, about 18 ms. I measured it as an attack. Customer A either sends a 4,096-token prompt or does not, at random. Then customer B sends the same prompt and times its first token. B wins if it can tell which happened. Over 400 trials:

With a shared cache the answer is not subtle. A hit returns in 16 ms and a miss in 179 ms, so one threshold is right every time. B does not even need a stopwatch: the response’s cached_tokens field says 4,095 when A was there.
The fix is to salt the cache per customer: mix a per-customer key into the tree, so that two requests only share a prefix if they share the key too.








Figure 21: The same four agents of two customers, without and with a per-customer salt. A salt keeps sharing inside a customer and stops it between customers.





SGLang’s /generate takes such a key as extra_key. With one per customer, B waits the same 182 ms either way, and its guess is right 53% of the time: a coin flip.

N_\text{max}(T) = \frac{\text{pool} - T \cdot S}{c - S}
\]

With a handful of customers per GPU, that costs a few agents, much less than sharing nothing. It is a cost to choose on purpose: put the salt on the customer, not on the user or the session. Salt per session and every agent carries its own copy, which is the 0% row of the earlier table.






Command: probing a shared cache, and salting it





import random, time, requests
URL = "http://localhost:30000"

def first_token(ids, key=None):
    body = {"input_ids": ids, "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 1}} | ({"extra_key": key} if key else {})
    t = time.perf_counter()
    r = requests.post(URL + "/generate", json=body).json()
    return time.perf_counter() - t, r["meta_info"]["cached_tokens"]

for salt in (False, True):
    right = 0
    for i in range(400):
        requests.post(URL + "/flush_cache")
        secret = [random.randrange(1000, 150_000) for _ in range(4096)]
        present = i % 2 == 0
        if present:
            first_token(secret, "customer-a" if salt else None)       # A sends it, or not
        wait, cached = first_token(secret, "customer-b" if salt else None)
        right += (wait < 0.08) == present                             # B guesses from the wait alone
    print("salted" if salt else "shared", right / 400)





Where this leaves me
Sharing is the one way to make a cache smaller without approximating anything, and on agent traffic there is exactly one thing to share: the prefix. Inside a session, the trace has no out-of-order repeats to recover. Across agents, the system prompt halves what each one holds, and keeping customers apart costs one copy of it per customer.
That still leaves each agent with its own 33K-token conversation, stored in 16-bit numbers. The next factor to attack is the bits.

title: Keeping 32 agents warm on one GPU
text:
Chapter 5: Fewer bits
Chapter 0 tried smaller numbers first and found they buy room: an FP8 cache holds twice the tokens, NVFP4 about 3.4 times. It left R4, quality, for later. Sharing has given all it can, so now R4 has to be measured.

How a number loses bits
A floating-point number is stored as a sign, an exponent and a mantissa: \(x = \pm\, 2^{e} \times 1.m\). The exponent sets the scale, and the mantissa sets the precision within that scale. BF16 has 8 exponent bits and 7 mantissa bits. The FP8 format SGLang uses, E4M3, has 4 and 3. That leaves two problems.

Precision. With 3 mantissa bits, neighbouring numbers are 1/8 apart in relative terms, so rounding moves a number by up to 1/16 of itself: about 6%.
Range. With 4 exponent bits, the largest E4M3 number is 448 and the smallest normal one is \(2^{-6} \approx 0.016\). Anything smaller loses precision fast, and anything larger does not fit.

To fit the range, numbers are divided by a scale \(s\) before rounding and multiplied back after:
\[
\hat{x} = s \cdot \text{round}_\text{E4M3}\!\left(\frac{x}{s}\right)
\]
A good \(s\) puts the largest number near the top of the range. One large number then forces a large \(s\), and every small number around it is pushed down toward the bottom of the range, where precision runs out. NVFP4 (E2M1) can only represent 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 6. It gets away with it by giving every block of 16 numbers its own scale, but within a block, one outlier sets the scale for the other 15.
So whether a cache survives fewer bits depends on how its numbers are spread out. That is something to measure.


How much change is “no measurable change”?
R4 says no measurable change, and that needs a yardstick. The model’s output is not perfectly repeatable even in BF16. GPU kernels add numbers in an order that depends on the batch, and floating-point addition is not associative: \((a + b) + c \neq a + (b + c)\) once rounding is involved. So I measured BF16 against itself first.
The measurement, Q1, compares the next-token probabilities two configurations give. Take 200 windows of real code (SGLang’s own source) between 1K and 128K tokens. Put each window in the cache, then feed the next 512 tokens of the file and record the model’s top-20 next-token probabilities at every one of them. At each position, the distance between the reference distribution \(p\) and the test distribution \(q\) is the KL divergence:
\[
D_\text{KL}(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_{x} p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}
\]
0 means identical. I only have the top 20 tokens of each, so I compute it over those tokens plus one bucket for everything else, which gives a lower bound on the full KL.
For the floor, both configurations are the same BF16 server, once with requests one at a time and once 16 at a time:

A small KL is not the same as a working agent, so I added a second check, Q2, for the task an agent actually does with a long context: find something it read earlier. Retrieval does not notice. Every format finds the same facts as BF16 to within a couple out of 100, which is the noise of a 100-question test. At these depths, a 4-bit cache still knows where everything is.
The probabilities do notice, and the two models react very differently. On Qwen3-8B, FP8 moves the model 2.0 times as far as R4 allows, and NVFP4 9 times. The damage grows with context: the more cached tokens a step reads, the more rounding error it adds up. Qwen3.5 passes with FP8 and misses by 19% with NVFP4, with no growth with context. That is the hybrid design again. Only 8 of Qwen3.5’s layers keep a cache, so only those 8 read rounded numbers. The cache format does not touch the DeltaNet states.


Keys or values?
Qwen3-8B fails even at FP8, so it is worth knowing where the error comes from. SGLang rounds keys and values together, so this one ran offline in plain PyTorch on Qwen3-8B: 50 windows of 8K tokens of code, with the keys, the values or both rounded to FP8 or NVFP4 before attention reads them, and the same KL against unrounded BF16. I tried two scales: \(s = 1\), which is what SGLang uses when it has no calibration, and one calibrated per layer from the largest number seen on 8 other windows.

It is the keys. Rounding only the values costs almost nothing in either format, and rounding only the keys costs nearly everything that rounding both does. My first guess was outliers, and the calibration pass recorded the range of both:








Figure 22: e5d, Qwen3-8B: the largest absolute key and value in each layer over 8 calibration windows of 8K tokens of code.





The guess is half right. In the first layers, keys do carry numbers hundreds of times bigger than the values: 234 against 0.5 in layer 0. But from layer 28 on, the largest values are bigger than the largest keys, and rounding values still costs almost nothing. So range is not what separates them. Where the error goes is.
An error in a key hurts more than the same error in a value. A key enters attention through a dot product with every query, and the result goes into an exponent:
\[
\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{q \cdot (k + \epsilon)}{\sqrt{H}}\right) \propto \exp\!\left(\frac{q \cdot k}{\sqrt{H}}\right) \cdot \exp\!\left(\frac{q \cdot \epsilon}{\sqrt{H}}\right)
\]
So a rounding error in \(k\) multiplies the attention weight, for every query that looks at it. A rounding error in \(v\) only adds a little noise to one term of an average, and averages forgive noise.
Calibrated scales help, but only by 22% for FP8. Applied to the served measurement, that would take Qwen3-8B’s FP8 from 7.4e-03 to about 5.7e-03, still above R4’s 3.6e-03. So I did not rerun the served test with calibrated scales.
Nor is there one bad layer that could stay in BF16. Rounding a single layer’s keys to NVFP4, the worst layer costs only 1.6× the median layer. The error is spread across the model.
The cheap option this points at is mixed formats, with values in 4 bits and keys in 8. SGLang 0.5.23 has one --kv-cache-dtype for both, so I could not serve it.


Where the cliff moves
Quality aside, does the room show up as agents? On the napkin, each format changes only the bytes-per-token term, so the cliff should move with the pool. I reran Chapter 2’s synthetic sweep in each format.

The first three rows are Chapter 2’s state pool again. Every run in this chapter used the 256 slots Chapter 2 chose, and Qwen3.5 has two pools with two limits. With \(R\) requests running and \(P\) agents parked:
\[
5R + P \le \text{slots}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\text{slots} \cdot \sigma + \text{tokens} \cdot b_\text{token} = \text{budget}
\]
The first says how many can run: at most 51 with 256 slots. The second says the two pools share one budget, so every slot costs as much memory as \(\sigma / b_\text{token}\) cached tokens. At 64 agents with NVFP4, 50 were running and 7 waiting, with the token pool only 80% full. Shrinking the tokens made more room in the pool that was not running out.
So the split has to move again. 256 slots were right when tokens were the scarce pool. With 512 slots, the token pool shrinks to 2.48 M, still room for 74 agents, and up to 102 requests can run. At 64 agents the hit rate went from 60% to 91%, and the median wait from 19 s to 0.38 s. That is the first configuration in this post where 64 agents fit.
They fit, but they do not yet pass. The p90 wait at 64 is 3.4 s, and each user gets 15 tokens/s: R2 and R3 still fail.

import requests
URL = "http://localhost:30000"

def tail_topk(context, continuation, k=20):

title: Keeping 32 agents warm on one GPU
text:
Chapter 6: Reading less
At 64 agents on Qwen3.5, each user gets 15 tokens/s. Chapter 0’s decode formula says why:
\[
t_\text{step}(B, S) = \frac{B \cdot (S \cdot b_\text{token} + 2\sigma)}{W} + \max\left(\frac{2BP}{C}, \frac{2P}{W}\right)
\]
Every step reads all the weights once, plus every running agent’s whole cache. At \(B\) = 64 agents of \(S\) = 69K tokens, in FP8, that is 94 GB per step, or 65 ms at the bandwidth Chapter 0 measured: at most 15 tokens/s per user, exactly what the run got. R3 wants 30. There are two ways to change the formula. Read fewer of the \(S\) tokens per step, or get more than one token out of each step.

Dropping tokens
The direct way to read less is to keep less. Token eviction throws away the cached tokens it guesses will not matter again, permanently. Two well-known guesses:

StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2024) keeps the first few tokens and a recent window. The first few matter because attention has to put its weight somewhere, and models learn to park spare weight on the first tokens (they are called attention sinks).
SnapKV (Li et al., 2024) keeps the recent window plus the older tokens that window attended to most. With \(a_{t,i}\) the attention token \(t\) pays to token \(i\), each old token is scored by \(\sum_{t \in \text{window}} a_{t,i}\), and the top ones stay.

An agent’s cache has to be compressed before its next turn exists, so I ran SnapKV without knowing the question: it scores the tokens by the attention of the context’s own last 32 tokens. SGLang does not evict tokens from inside a sequence, so this ran offline in PyTorch on Qwen3-8B, with 32K-token windows of code and the same KL as Chapter 5.




Table 38

Nothing here passes R4 (3.6e-03). SnapKV at half the cache moves the model 2.4 times as far as allowed, about what FP8 did for the same 2× saving, and it gets much worse below half. StreamingLLM ignores what is in the context and is worse at every budget. Agent contexts do not have a recent part that matters and an old part that does not: the file read twenty turns ago is still the file being edited.



Reading only what matters
Eviction makes its guess once and lives with it. Sparse attention keeps the whole cache in memory and, at each step, reads only the parts that step needs. That saves no memory. It attacks the reads, which are what R3 is short of.
The bet is that attention is concentrated. If the blocks a step reads capture most of its attention weight, the output barely changes, because the output is a weighted average of values and the skipped ones had little weight. Write \(m_k\) for the share of attention the best \(k\) blocks capture:
\[
m_k = \sum_{i \in \text{top-}k \text{ blocks}} a_{t,i}
\]
How far could that go, in the best case? I measured it with an oracle. At each of 32 decode steps over a 32K-token context, I computed the real attention, picked the \(k\) 64-token blocks that got the most of it in each layer, and reran the step with attention restricted to those blocks.

Reading 12.5% of the context, the right 4,096 tokens, captures 93% of the attention and moves the model by 1.9e-03, inside R4. That is about the change FP8 made to Qwen3.5, for an eighth of the cache reads. Using an eighth is far better than keeping half, because the right eighth is different at every step, and eviction has to pick one set for all of them.
But it is an oracle. It needs the full attention to know which blocks to read, and the full attention is the read it is trying to avoid. Real sparse-attention methods guess the blocks from a cheap summary of each one, and they will miss some of that mass. SGLang 0.5.23 has nothing like it for these two models, so on this stack the saving stays on paper.


More tokens per read
The other way is to make each step produce more than one token. Qwen3.5 ships with a small extra head trained to guess the next few tokens (multi-token prediction). In speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), that head drafts \(d\) tokens, and one step of the big model checks all of them at once: it computes what it would have written at each of the \(d + 1\) positions and keeps the drafts up to the first one it disagrees with. When most drafts are accepted, one read of the weights and the cache yields several tokens. With \(a\) tokens kept per step,
\[
\text{tokens/s per user} = \frac{a}{t_\text{step}}
\]
and the step costs about the same as a normal one, as long as checking \(d + 1\) tokens instead of one does not run out of compute.

At 32 at a time, the server finished 1.0 requests per second, and prefilling their prompts alone needs 68% of the GPU’s compute. Checking 5 tokens instead of 1 then costs compute the GPU does not have.
Speculation also takes memory: the draft head and its own cache shrank the token pool from 1.64 M to 0.99 M. For many agents on one GPU, it is the wrong trade. For a few agents that need to be fast, it is the best one in this post.

The same run also timed 8K and 32K contexts, but two of those points disagree with Chapter 0’s measurements of the same thing, so I left them out until I know why.






Command: speculative decoding with Qwen3.5’s own draft head





python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B \
  --context-length 131072 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --enable-metrics \
  --speculative-algorithm NEXTN --speculative-draft-model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B \
  --speculative-num-steps 4 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 5
The response’s meta_info reports spec_accept_length, the tokens kept per step. The server also caps running requests at 48 when speculation is on, and says so in its log.





Where a Qwen3.5 fork can start
Chapter 0 left a warning: a DeltaNet state is a blend of everything before it, so Qwen3.5 can only resume from a point where a snapshot was saved. Chapter 3’s forks all branched at the end of a turn, where one always is. A sub-agent can also branch from the middle of one, for example right after the planner wrote its plan but before the tool output that followed. I built a 4-turn parent with 4,096-token turns and forked it at positions on and off turn boundaries.




Table 42

Qwen3-8B reuses the parent’s cache up to the exact token. Qwen3.5 reuses it only up to the last turn boundary, whatever snapshot interval I set: --mamba-track-interval of 64, 256 and 1024 tokens all gave the same row. The warning came true. SGLang saved a state at the end of each request, not every 64 tokens, and a fork inside the first turn reuses nothing at all.


Where this leaves me
The reads are the problem now, and on this stack they stay the problem. Dropping tokens fails R4 at any budget worth having. Reading only the right tokens would work, but only an oracle knows which they are, and SGLang does not offer the approximation for these models. Speculation helps a single agent by 2.5× and many agents not at all.
That leaves one direction from Chapter 2 untried: putting the caches that do not fit somewhere bigger than GPU memory.

title: Keeping 32 agents warm on one GPU
text:
Chapter 7: Bigger than GPU memory
Chapter 0 measured two places bigger than GPU memory (Table 10): this machine’s 176 GB of CPU memory, behind a 57 GB/s link, and a disk at 1.7 GB/s. Chapter 3 showed what needs them: the caches of parked agents, which the GPU pool keeps evicting. SGLang can put both behind the pool as tiers (--enable-hierarchical-cache). A cache evicted from the GPU is kept in CPU memory, and when its agent comes back, it is copied back instead of recomputed.
Whether that pays is a race between a copy and a rebuild. For an agent returning with \(c\) private tokens:
\[
t_\text{copy} = \frac{c \cdot b_\text{token}}{W_\text{link}}
\qquad\text{vs}\qquad
t_\text{rebuild} = \frac{\text{FLOPs}_\text{prefill}(c \mid S \text{ cached})}{C}
\]
For one synthetic agent’s 33K private tokens on Qwen3-8B, the copy moves 4.9 GB:








Figure 26: Napkin, from p0-micro’s link and disk bandwidth and Chapter 0’s prefill formula: time to bring one synthetic agent’s private context back into GPU memory, Qwen3-8B, BF16.





CPU memory wins by a mile. The disk is roughly a wash with recomputing.

CPU memory
--hicache-ratio sets the CPU pool’s size as a multiple of the GPU pool’s. I ran Chapter 2’s synthetic sweep with ratios 1 and 2 on both models, out to 96 agents.








Figure 27: e2a, e2d and e8a, synthetic traffic (seed 0), BF16 cache, Qwen3.5 with 256 state slots: median wait against agents at once, by CPU pool size. The dotted line is 1 s.









Table 43







CPU pool
Hit rate at 16 / 32 / 48 / 64 / 96 agents




Qwen3-8B
none

Qwen3-8B
1 × GPU pool
88% / 57% / 53% / 61% / –


Qwen3-8B

none

Qwen3.5-9B
1 × GPU pool
93% / 94% / 88% / 68% / 59%


Qwen3.5-9B
2 × GPU pool
93% / 94% / 94% / 94% / 93%








Ratio 1 does almost nothing for Qwen3-8B, and that is by design. By default SGLang copies every page to the CPU pool as soon as it is computed (write-through), so the CPU pool holds a copy of the GPU pool before it holds anything else. With a GPU pool \(G\) and ratio \(r\), what the two tiers hold between them is
\[
\text{unique capacity}_\text{write-through} = G + (r - 1)\,G = r\,G
\]
At ratio 1, that is just \(G\): the copy is all it holds. At ratio 2 there is a second pool’s worth of room, and the hit rate holds at 91% out to 32 agents, where without it the cliff was at 16.
The hits did not bring the wait down, though: 42 s at 32 agents. That is Chapter 3’s lesson from the other side. CPU memory can keep a parked agent’s cache. But a running request still needs its whole context in GPU memory, and Qwen3-8B’s GPU pool runs about 13 synthetic agents at a time. Past that they queue, cache or no cache. The CPU tier turns their rebuild into a copy. It does not give them a seat.
Qwen3.5 has the bigger GPU pool, so it gets the seats. With ratio 2 it keeps a 94% hit rate and a 0.6 s median wait at 64 agents, in BF16 with the old 256 state slots. At 96 it queues again: 51 running at most, Chapter 5’s limit. Ratio 1 already helped at 48 agents on Qwen3.5, which the write-through copy does not explain. I have not looked into why.


When to copy
If write-through spends the CPU pool on copies, the policy should matter. --hicache-write-policy has three settings. Write-through copies every page. Write-through-selective copies only pages that have been hit a few times. Write-back copies a page only when the GPU evicts it, so the CPU pool holds nothing the GPU still has:
\[
\text{unique capacity}_\text{write-back} = G + r\,G
\]
Same point, 48 agents on Qwen3-8B, ratio 2:




Table 44






Write policy
Unique capacity, GPU + CPU
Hit rate
Median wait




write-through (default)

G + the pages hit often
51%

write-back

90%

Write-back turns the same CPU memory into half again as much unique capacity, and the hit rate goes from 70% to 90%. Selective is the worst of the three. My reading is that an agent’s cache is used by one agent a few times, so “hit often” rarely singles one out, and most of them never reach the CPU pool at all. The wait improved too, 196 s to 150 s, but it is still minutes, for the reason above: 48 agents is far past what Qwen3-8B can run at once.
For agents, the default is the wrong choice. Write-through’s advantage is that a page already has its copy when the GPU evicts it, so eviction never waits on the link.


The disk
Below CPU memory, SGLang’s file backend writes pages to disk and prefetches them back when a request matches them. --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy decides whether a request waits for the whole prefetch (wait_complete), takes what has arrived (best_effort), or waits up to a timeout. I ran 48 and 96 agents on Qwen3-8B with a CPU pool of ratio 1 and the disk behind it.

The disk changed nothing, which is what Figure 26 said: a page from disk costs about what recomputing it does, and these agents are queued for seats anyway.
One caveat on this run. SGLang ignores its own flags for where the file backend writes, and takes the directory only from the environment variable SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_STORAGE_DIR. Without it, pages go to /tmp/hicache, which here grew to 415 GB, and my harness emptied a different directory between policies. So the second and third policies started with the first one’s pages on disk. That can only have helped them, and they still gained nothing.






Command: CPU and disk tiers





export SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_STORAGE_DIR=/data/hicache   # otherwise /tmp/hicache, with no size limit
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  --json-model-override-args '{"rope_scaling":{"rope_type":"yarn","factor":4.0,"original_max_position_embeddings":32768},"max_position_embeddings":131072}' \
  --context-length 131072 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --enable-metrics \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 2 --hicache-write-policy write_back \
  --hicache-storage-backend file --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete   # the disk tier; drop for CPU only
The response’s meta_info.cached_tokens_details splits each hit into device, host and storage tokens.

title: Training LLMs to Think
text:
am.
  
    Writing
    Work
    Projects
    Talks
It’s been a while since I wrote a blog on slightly technical topic. Today is the day!
It’s 2025 and LLMs have gained ability to “reason” their way through a tricky math problems. It’s not magic—it’s the result of specialized post-training. While pre-trained LLMs are incredibly knowledgeable, they aren’t born problem-solvers. To get them to excel at complex tasks like mathematical reasoning, we need to fine-tune them.
In this guide, we’ll learn how to do just that. We’re going to take a powerful base model, Qwen3-1.7B-Base, and teach it to reason using a clever RL technique called GRPO and the speed-boosting Unsloth library. Let’s get started!

title: Training LLMs to Think
text:
Why Use Unsloth?

Unsloth is a powerful library designed to make fine-tuning LLMs faster and more memory-efficient. It achieves this through several optimizations, including:

Faster training: Unsloth can significantly speed up the training process, in some cases by a factor of 2x or more.
Reduced memory usage: It allows for fine-tuning larger models on consumer-grade hardware by reducing the memory footprint.
Ease of use: Unsloth provides a user-friendly API that simplifies the fine-tuning workflow.

Now, let’s dive into the code and the fine-tuning process.

title: Training LLMs to Think
text:
The Post Training Process

1. Setting Up the Environment
The first step is to install the necessary libraries. The script provides commands for both a standard Python environment and a Google Colab instance.

Standard EnvironmentGoogle Colab


# For a standard environment
!pip install unsloth vllm


!pip install --no-deps unsloth vllm==0.8.5.post1
!pip install --no-deps bitsandbytes accelerate xformers==0.0.29.post3 peft trl triton cut_cross_entropy unsloth_zoo
!pip install sentencepiece protobuf "datasets>=3.4.1,<4.0.0>" "huggingface_hub>=0.34.0" hf_transfer



These commands install Unsloth for post-training, vLLM for fast inference, and other essential libraries like PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning), TRL (Transformer Reinforcement Learning), and Datasets.


2. Loading the Model and Preparing for PEFT
Next, we load the Qwen3-1.7B-Base model using Unsloth’s FastLanguageModel. We also configure it for PEFT using LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation).
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel
import torch

max_seq_length = 2048
lora_rank = 32

model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name = "unsloth/Qwen3-1.7B-Base",
    max_seq_length = max_seq_length,
    load_in_4bit = False, # False for LoRA 16bit
    fast_inference = True, # Enable vLLM fast inference
    max_lora_rank = lora_rank,
    gpu_memory_utilization = 0.7, # Reduce if out of memory
)

model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(
    model,
    r = lora_rank, # Choose any number > 0 ! Suggested 8, 16, 32, 64, 128
    target_modules = [
        "q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",
        "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj",
    ],
    lora_alpha = lora_rank*2, # *2 speeds up training
    use_gradient_checkpointing = "unsloth", # Reduces memory usage
    random_state = 3407,
)






Note




FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained: This function from Unsloth loads the model and tokenizer with optimizations for speed and memory.
max_seq_length: This defines the maximum number of tokens the model can handle in a single input.
lora_rank: This is a key parameter for LoRA. It determines the rank of the matrices that are used to approximate the weight updates. A larger rank can lead to a more “intelligent” model but at the cost of slower training and higher memory usage.
get_peft_model: This function prepares the model for PEFT by adding LoRA adapters to the specified target_modules.
lora_alpha: This is a scaling factor for the LoRA updates. Think of lora_alpha as controlling how much importance is given to the new, fine-tuned weights versus the original model weights. Setting it to twice the lora_rank is a common heuristic that provides a good starting point for stable training.





3. Crafting a Custom Chat Template for GRPO
Before we can train our model, we need to teach it how to structure its responses. We do this by defining a chat template. This template acts as a blueprint, guiding the model to generate output in a consistent, predictable format that is ideal for our reasoning task.






What is a Chat Template?



Most Large Language Models are, at their core, text-completion engines. They don’t inherently understand the back-and-forth nature of a conversation. A chat template is a set of rules that tells the tokenizer how to convert a structured list of messages (from a “user” and “assistant”) into a single, formatted string the model can process.
Instruction-tuned models (like Llama-3-Instruct) already have a built-in template. Since we are using a base model, it has no default conversational format, so we must create our own.


Our goal is to create a template that forces the model to “show its work” and provide a clear final answer. To do this, we’ll build the template in three main steps.

Step 1 : Define the Structure with Special Tokens
First, we’ll define the special tags that will act as dividers in the model’s output. This allows our reward functions to easily parse the response later.
# Define the special tokens that will structure the output
reasoning_start = "<think>"
reasoning_end   = "</think>"
solution_start  = "<SOLUTION>"
solution_end    = "</SOLUTION>"
Our desired output format will look like this:
<think>
...the model's step-by-step reasoning goes here...
</think>
<SOLUTION>
...the model's final answer goes here...
</SOLUTION>


Step 2 : Create the System Prompt and Jinja Template
Next, we create the instructions for the model. This involves two parts: a high-level system prompt telling the model its role, and a Jinja2 template that programmatically assembles the conversation for the model.
# Create the system prompt that instructs the model on the format
system_prompt = \
f"""You are given a problem.
Think about the problem and provide your working out.
Place it between {reasoning_start} and {reasoning_end}.
Then, provide your solution between {solution_start}{solution_end}"""

# Define the Jinja2 template for the tokenizer
chat_template = \
    "{% if messages[0]['role'] == 'system' %}"\
        "{{ messages[0]['content'] + eos_token }}"\
        "{% set loop_messages = messages[1:] %}"\
    "{% else %}"\
        "{{ '{system_prompt}' + eos_token }}"\
        "{% set loop_messages = messages %}"\
    "{% endif %}"\
    "{% for message in loop_messages %}"\
        "{% if message['role'] == 'user' %}"\
            "{{ message['content'] }}"\
        "{% elif message['role'] == 'assistant' %}"\
            "{{ message['content'] + eos_token }}"\
        "{% endif %}"\
    "{% endfor %}"\
    "{% if add_generation_prompt %}{{ '{reasoning_start}' }}"\
    "{% endif %}"
The Jinja template is the core logic. It loops through the conversation history and formats it correctly. The most important line is the last one: {% if add_generation_prompt %}. This tells the tokenizer to automatically add our <think> token whenever it’s the model’s turn to speak, kicking off the required reasoning process.


Step 3: Apply the Template to the Tokenizer
Finally, we inject our custom system_prompt into the Jinja template and assign the completed template to our tokenizer. This makes our custom format the official rulebook for all future conversations.
# Inject our custom system prompt and starting token into the template
chat_template = chat_template\
    .replace("'{system_prompt}'",   f"'{system_prompt}'")\
    .replace("'{reasoning_start}'", f"'{reasoning_start}'")

# Finally, apply this template to the tokenizer
tokenizer.chat_template = chat_template
By enforcing this structure, we make the process of rewarding the model for good reasoning both programmatic and reliable. It’s the foundation upon which our entire GRPO training strategy is built.



4. Pre-Finetuning for Formatting
Before we let the model learn through trial-and-error with GRPO, we first give it a head start with a short phase of Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). Why? Reinforcement learning is most effective when the model already has a rough idea of what to do. If a base model has never seen our <think> format, it will generate random, unstructured text. Rewarding the rare occasions it gets the format right is highly inefficient.
This SFT step acts as behavioral cloning. We show the model a few hundred examples of the exact format we want. This quickly teaches it the basic structure, making the subsequent GRPO phase much more stable and focused on improving the reasoning within the format, rather than just learning the format itself.
We use a small subset of NVIDIA’s Open Math Reasoning dataset for this.

Loading and Formatting the SFT Dataset
First, we load the dataset using Hugging Face’s datasets library. We’ll filter it to only include problems with numerical answers to keep things simple for this pre-tuning step.
from datasets import load_dataset
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

dataset = load_dataset("unsloth/OpenMathReasoning-mini", split = "cot")
dataset = dataset.to_pandas()[
    ["expected_answer", "problem", "generated_solution"]
]

# Keep only samples where the answer is a number
is_number = pd.to_numeric(pd.Series(dataset["expected_answer"]), errors = "coerce").notnull()
dataset = dataset.iloc[np.where(is_number)[0]]
Next, we create a function to reformat each row into the custom chat structure we defined earlier. This function takes the existing reasoning trace and wraps it with our special tokens (, , etc.).
def format_sft_dataset(x):
    # Reformat the existing solution to match our template
    thoughts = x["generated_solution"].replace("<think>", "").replace("</think>", "").strip()
    
    # Construct the final response format
    final_prompt = \
        reasoning_start + thoughts + reasoning_end + \
        solution_start + x["expected_answer"] + solution_end
    
    # Return the message structure
    return [
        {"role" : "system",    "content" : system_prompt},
        {"role" : "user",      "content" : x["problem"]},
        {"role" : "assistant", "content" : final_prompt},
    ]

dataset["Messages"] = dataset.apply(format_sft_dataset, axis = 1)
Finally, we convert our pandas DataFrame back into a Hugging Face Dataset object, which the SFTTrainer expects.
from datasets import Dataset

dataset["text"] = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    dataset["Messages"].values.tolist(), tokenize = False
)
dataset = Dataset.from_pandas(dataset)
Now that our dataset is prepared, we can pass it to the SFTTrainer.
import numpy as np
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig

# Load and format the dataset from the original script
# This involves loading "unsloth/OpenMathReasoning-mini", filtering,
# and applying the format_dataset function.

# Create the SFT Trainer
trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model = model,
    tokenizer = tokenizer,
    train_dataset = dataset, # The formatted dataset
    args = SFTConfig(
        dataset_text_field = "text",
        per_device_train_batch_size = 1,
        gradient_accumulation_steps = 1, # Use GA to mimic batch size!
        warmup_steps = 5,
        num_train_epochs = 2, # Set this for 1 full training run.
        learning_rate = 2e-4, # Reduce to 2e-5 for long training runs
        logging_steps = 5,
        optim = "adamw_8bit",
        weight_decay = 0.01,
        lr_scheduler_type = "linear",
        seed = 3407,
        report_to = "none", # Use "wandb" for Weights & Biases
    ),
)

# Start the pre-finetuning
trainer.train()
We map the dataset to create a “prompt” which includes our system message and the user’s question, and an “answer” which is the expected solution.



5. Defining the Reward System
With the model primed on formatting, it’s time to set up the main GRPO training loop. This starts with preparing our primary dataset and defining the reward functions that will guide the learning process.

Loading the GRPO Dataset
For the main RL phase, we’ll use the open-r1/DAPO-Math-17k-Processed dataset. We’ll map it to a simple structure containing the prompt and the ground-truth answer.
from datasets import load_dataset

# Load the main dataset for GRPO
dataset = load_dataset("open-r1/DAPO-Math-17k-Processed", "en", split = "train")

# Map it to our required format
dataset = dataset.map(lambda x: {
    "prompt" : [
        {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
        {"role": "user",   "content": x["prompt"]},
    ],
    "answer": x["solution"],
})

Reward Functions
The core of GRPO is scoring the model’s generated outputs. We’ll use the four reward functions. The GRPOTrainer sums the scores from all of them to get a final reward for each generation.

match_format_exactly: We give a large positive reward to modelif the response perfectly follows our defined structure. We can use a regular expression to check if the , , , and  tags appear in the correct order.

import re

# We pre-compile regex for efficiency
solution_end_regex = r"</SOLUTION>[\s]{0,}" + "(?:" + re.escape(tokenizer.eos_token) + ")?"
match_format = re.compile(
    rf"{reasoning_end}.*?{solution_start}(.+?){solution_end_regex}",
    flags = re.MULTILINE | re.DOTALL
)

def match_format_exactly(completions, **kwargs):
    scores = []
    for completion in completions:
        score = 0
        response = completion[0]["content"]
        # Match if format is seen exactly!
        if match_format.search(response) is not None: score += 3.0
        scores.append(score)
    return scores

match_format_approximately: If the format isn’t perfect, we should gives partial credit to model. To do this, we check for the presence of each required tag (, , ) and add a small reward for each one found, while penalizing the model if a tag is missing. This encourages the model to at least try to follow the format.

def match_format_approximately(completions, **kwargs):
    scores = []
    for completion in completions:
        score = 0
        response = completion[0]["content"]
        # Count how many keywords are seen - we penalize if too many!
        score += 0.5 if response.count(reasoning_end)   == 1 else -1.0
        score += 0.5 if response.count(solution_start)  == 1 else -1.0
        score += 0.5 if response.count(solution_end)    == 1 else -1.0
        scores.append(score)
    return scores

check_answer: With this reward function assesses the correctness of the answer. We first tries to extract the text within the  tags. If the format is wrong, we assigns a penalty. If the format is correct, we compare the extracted text to the ground-truth answer, giving a high reward for an exact match. We also provides a partial reward if the numerical ratio between the guessed answer and the true answer is close (e.g., within 10% or 20%).


def check_answer(prompts, completions, answer, **kwargs):
    question = prompts[0][-1]["content"]
    responses = [completion[0]["content"] for completion in completions]

    extracted_responses = [
        guess.group(1)
        if (guess := match_format.search(r)) is not None else None \
        for r in responses
    ]

    scores = []
    for guess, true_answer in zip(extracted_responses, answer):
        score = 0
        if guess is None:
            scores.append(-2.0)
            continue
        # Correct answer gets 5 points!
        if guess == true_answer:
            score += 5.0
        # Match if spaces are seen, but less reward
        elif guess.strip() == true_answer.strip():
            score += 3.5
        else:
            # We also reward it if the answer is close via ratios!
            # Ie if the answer is within some range, reward it!
            try:
                ratio = float(guess) / float(true_answer)
                if   ratio >= 0.9 and ratio <= 1.1: score += 2.0
                elif ratio >= 0.8 and ratio <= 1.2: score += 1.5
                else: score -= 2.5 # Penalize wrong answers
            except:
                score -= 4.5 # Penalize
        scores.append(score)
    return scores

check_numbers - We also provide an additional reward specifically for numerical answers. To do this we extract only the numbers from the solution, clean them up (e.g., removes commas), convert them to floats, and give a positive reward for an exact numerical match or a penalty otherwise.

match_numbers = re.compile(
    solution_start + r".*?[\s]{0,}([-]?[\d\.\,]{1,})",
    flags = re.MULTILINE | re.DOTALL
)

global PRINTED_TIMES
PRINTED_TIMES = 0
global PRINT_EVERY_STEPS
PRINT_EVERY_STEPS = 5

def check_numbers(prompts, completions, answer, **kwargs):
    question = prompts[0][-1]["content"]
    responses = [completion[0]["content"] for completion in completions]
    extracted_responses = [
        guess.group(1) if (guess := match_numbers.search(r)) is not None else None \
        for r in responses
    ]
    scores = []
    global PRINTED_TIMES, PRINT_EVERY_STEPS
    if PRINTED_TIMES % PRINT_EVERY_STEPS == 0:
        print(f"*****\nQ: {question}\nA: {answer[0]}\nR: {responses[0]}\nE: {extracted_responses[0]}\n*****")
    PRINTED_TIMES += 1

    for guess, true_answer in zip(extracted_responses, answer):
        if guess is None:
            scores.append(-2.5)
            continue
        try:
            true_num = float(true_answer.strip())
            guess_num = float(guess.strip().replace(",", ""))
            scores.append(3.5 if guess_num == true_num else -1.5)
        except:
            scores.append(0)
    return scores
By combining these reward functions, we create a comprehensive scoring system that encourages the model to generate well-structured and accurate responses.




6. Configuring and Launching the GRPO Trainer
Now, we configure the GRPOTrainer with our model, tokenizer, reward functions, and training arguments.
from trl import GRPOConfig, GRPOTrainer
from vllm import SamplingParams

# Define sampling parameters for vLLM
vllm_sampling_params = SamplingParams(
    min_p = 0.1,
    top_p = 1.0,
    top_k = -1,
    seed = 3407,
    stop = [tokenizer.eos_token],
    include_stop_str_in_output = True,
)

# Configure GRPO training
training_args = GRPOConfig(
    vllm_sampling_params = vllm_sampling_params,
    temperature = 1.0,
    learning_rate = 5e-6,
    weight_decay = 0.01,
    warmup_ratio = 0.1,
    lr_scheduler_type = "linear",
    optim = "adamw_8bit",
    logging_steps = 1,
    per_device_train_batch_size = 1,
    gradient_accumulation_steps = 1, # Increase for smoother training
    num_generations = 4, # Decrease if out of memory
    max_prompt_length = max_prompt_length,
    max_completion_length = max_completion_length,
    max_steps = 100, # Set to a higher number for a full run
    save_steps = 100,
    report_to = "none", # Can use "wandb"
    output_dir = "outputs",
)






Key GRPOConfig Parameters




num_generations: This is the ‘G’ in GRPO—the size of the group of responses generated for each prompt. A larger group gives better statistics for the advantage calculation but uses more memory and compute. A value of 4-8 is a good starting point.
temperature: A higher temperature (like 1.0) encourages the model to generate more diverse and creative responses for the group. This diversity is essential for exploration, as it allows the model to try different reasoning paths. A low temperature would make all the responses in the group too similar, hindering learning.



# Initialize the trainer
trainer = GRPOTrainer(
    model = model,
    processing_class = tokenizer,
    reward_funcs = [
        match_format_exactly,
        match_format_approximately,
        check_answer,
        check_numbers,
    ],
    args = training_args,
    train_dataset = dataset,
)

# Start training!
trainer.train()
The GRPOTrainer uses the configuration to fine-tune the model. The goal during training is to see the reward column in the training logs increase over time.


7. Inference with the Fine-tuned Model
After training, we can test our fine-tuned model. First, we save the trained LoRA adapter, then load it during inference.
# Save the LoRA adapter
model.save_lora("grpo_saved_lora")

# Prepare messages for inference
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
    {"role": "user",   "content": "What is the sqrt of 101?"},
]

text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt = True, # Must add for generation
    tokenize = False,
)

# Generate text using the fine-tuned LoRA
output = model.fast_generate(
    text,
    sampling_params = sampling_params,
    lora_request = model.load_lora("grpo_saved_lora"),
)[0].outputs[0].text

print(output)
The lora_request argument tells the model to use our fine-tuned LoRA adapter for this generation. The output should now follow the reasoning format we defined.


8. Saving and Sharing Your Model
Finally, Unsloth provides convenient methods for saving your fine-tuned model in various formats.

Saving as a merged model (float16 or 4-bit):Saving just the LoRA adaptersConverting to GGUF for llama.cpp


# This combines the base model with the LoRA adapter into a single model.


# Merge to 16-bit
model.save_pretrained_merged(
    "model", 
    tokenizer, 
    save_method = "merged_16bit"
)

# Merge to 4-bit
model.save_pretrained_merged(
    "model", 
    tokenizer, 
    save_method = "merged_4bit"
)


# Merge to 16-bit
model.save_pretrained_merged(
    "model", 
    tokenizer, 
    save_method = "merged_16bit"
)

# Merge to 4-bit
model.save_pretrained_merged(
    "model", 
    tokenizer, 
    save_method = "merged_4bit"
)


# Save to 8-bit Q8_0 GGUF
model.save_pretrained_gguf("model", tokenizer)

# Save to q4_k_m GGUF
model.save_pretrained_gguf("model", tokenizer, quantization_method = "q4_k_m")

title: Training LLMs to Think
text:
Closing Note
That’s it! Now you know the fundamentals of fancy “post-training”. You see how easy it is create specialized models that excel at complex tasks by combining a powerful base model, a clever reinforcement learning technique, and an efficient library.






Key Takeaways




GRPO is an effective method for teaching models to reason by rewarding them for correct and well-structured responses.
Unsloth makes the fine-tuning process more accessible by improving speed and reducing memory usage.
A well-defined reward system is crucial for the success of GRPO.
Pre-finetuning can help to streamline the main RL training phase.

title: Does RL in autoregressive decoding move the benchmark needle in diffusion decoding?
text:
am.
  
    Writing
    Work
    Projects
    Talks
First things first, this new model by NVIDIA, Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-3B, blew my mind. It can generate text in two ways: one token at a time, like a regular language model (autoregressive, or AR mode), and several tokens at once (diffusion mode). Both modes use the same model weights.
The speed is what excites me. But I haven’t come across a post-training recipe for diffusion transformers that feels mainstream yet. How do I take one of these fast models and make it better at a task?
We already have recipes for post-training autoregressive models. What if I post-train this model in AR mode, then switch it back to diffusion? Does any of that improvement carry over?
If it does, that would be insanely valuable: I could use a familiar training setup to improve the model, then use its faster diffusion mode to generate answers. That could be extremely useful in production applications, where I want a model that’s good at the task and responds quickly. Of course, sharing weights doesn’t guarantee that the gains transfer.

title: Does RL in autoregressive decoding move the benchmark needle in diffusion decoding?
text:
Experiment design
For this run, I use reinforcement learning (RL) to train only the AR mode. I save checkpoints along the way and try each one in both modes. Step 0 is the original model, before any training.
I wanted problems with room to improve and answers I could check automatically.
The tech report reports 87.9% on GSM8K in AR mode and 88.4% in diffusion mode for the 3B instruct model. There’s less room to improve there, so I kept GSM8K as a check and looked for harder problems to train on.
For MATH, I tried 300 problems each from Levels 3, 4 and 5 of the test set in AR mode:



MATH level
AR accuracy




Level 3
84.3%


Level 4
75.7%


Level 5
59.3%



Level 5 it is. Diffusion mode on the same 300 problems got 56.3% using NVIDIA’s HF implementation. Those probe scores helped me pick the task; the larger checkpoint sweep below uses SGLang for diffusion.
Here’s the training and eval setup:



Part of the experiment
Setup




Model
Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-3B


Training
AR-only RL on MATH train Levels 4 and 5: 3,994 problems


Testing on MATH
500 MATH Level-5 problems from the test split


Checking GSM8K
200 GSM8K test questions, outside the training dataset


Checkpoints evaluated
Original model, then steps 25, 50, 75, 100, 125 and 150



I didn’t train on GSM8K. I keep those questions around to check whether training on MATH also changes how the model handles another set of problems, especially whether it makes those answers worse.
Each checkpoint gets the same test questions, with greedy decoding and one answer per question. I count how many answers are right. For MATH, math-verify parses the prediction and checks it against the gold solution. For GSM8K, I check the last number in the last <answer> tag, falling back to the last number in the output if the tag is missing.
The instructions go in a single user message; I don’t add a custom system prompt. For MATH, I use the same prompt during training and evaluation in both modes:
{problem}

Think step by step, then put the final answer in \boxed{}.
For the GSM8K check:
{question}

Think step by step, then give the final number inside <answer> </answer> tags.
Both use the model’s chat template with enable_thinking=False.
I shuffle the MATH test questions with seed 1234 before selecting them; GSM8K keeps its original test order. The pinned revisions are 0530c786 for MATH, 740312ad for GSM8K and 0d51902d for the model. AR runs through vLLM, diffusion through SGLang. Each mode keeps the same engine and settings across checkpoints.

title: Does RL in autoregressive decoding move the benchmark needle in diffusion decoding?
text:
Training setup
Before getting to GRPO, it helps to unpack how this model can do both jobs. In the paper, NVIDIA trains a shared transformer with two objectives: predict the next token from the tokens before it, and recover missing tokens inside a block. The same weights learn both.






Figure 1: The embeddings, transformer blocks and vocabulary projection are shared. The mode changes attention and how token scores become an answer.



The attention mask controls which tokens can see each other:

AR mode: causal attention limits each position to itself and earlier positions; the model predicts the next token from that prefix. Generation proceeds left to right.
Diffusion mode: positions inside the current block can attend to each other and the completed prefix. The model fills masked positions over several passes, committing confident predictions. Blocks still finish in order; the whole answer isn’t generated at once. I use 32-token blocks here.







Figure 2: Colored cells show allowed attention. The diffusion block can look within itself, while the completed prefix stays causal. Four positions per block are drawn here; the experiment uses 32.



The paper calls this a tri-mode model because it also supports self-speculation: diffusion drafts tokens and AR verifies them. This experiment uses the two modes separately.
For the 3B checkpoint, the implementation wraps a Ministral3 transformer and an output layer that turns its hidden states into scores over the vocabulary. That transformer is stored under encoder, and the output layer under diffusion_head. Both are used by the AR path too, despite those names.
Now the practical problem: I’m using TRL’s GRPO trainer with vLLM to generate the training answers. I need those tools to load the checkpoint as a causal language model. NVIDIA ships a custom model class with its own AR and diffusion generation methods, so I can’t just point my usual training setup at it and assume it’ll work.
But I only need the AR path for training. Since that path uses the Ministral3 backbone, I can save the weights in the layout expected by Ministral3ForCausalLM, which my training stack can load.






Figure 3: Only the GRPO step updates weight values. Exporting and restoring the checkpoint change its layout so the training and evaluation tools can load it.









What the conversion changes



The conversion renames the weight keys and writes a matching Ministral3 model config:



NVIDIA checkpoint
AR checkpoint used by the trainer




encoder.*
model.*


diffusion_head.*
lm_head.*



The weight values and tokenizer stay the same. This export gives the trainer the AR view of the model; it doesn’t provide diffusion generation. To evaluate a trained checkpoint in diffusion mode, I reverse the names and load the updated weights with NVIDIA’s original config and model code.


Before training, I checked the original AR path against the converted model on the same prompt. The largest logit difference was 0.0, and greedy decoding produced the same tokens. That check gave me confidence to use the converted checkpoint for the run. GRPO then updates those shared weights through AR answers; afterward, I load them back into the original model to see what happened to diffusion.
The RL itself is plain GRPO in TRL, with vLLM generating the rollouts:

64 problems per step, 8 answers each, so 512 rollouts per step
learning rate 1e-6, no KL penalty, temperature 1.0, up to 2,048 tokens per answer
reward is 1 for a correct answer, 0 otherwise
a checkpoint every 25 steps

VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 uv run accelerate launch --config_file configs/fsdp8.yaml -m dar.train_grpo \
  --task math --run-name math-ar-grpo \
  --hypothesis "RL in AR mode also raises diffusion-mode accuracy on the same task" --vllm-mem 0.4

title: Does RL in autoregressive decoding move the benchmark needle in diffusion decoding?
text:
The training run
Training took about 34 seconds per step. I planned 200 steps, but the trainer’s own check (AR mode, 128 test problems, one sampled answer each) went flat around step 100, so I stopped it after 164 logged training steps. The last checkpoint is step 150.




                        
                                            


Figure 4: Top: mean reward on the training rollouts (10-step rolling mean), which is the share of the 512 sampled answers per step that were right. Bottom: mean answer length in tokens. Both come from the training batch, not the test set.




The reward goes from about 0.62 over the first 10 steps to about 0.74 after step 100. The answers also get a lot longer, from about 735 tokens to about 1,100. By steps 51 to 100, about 21% of the rollouts were hitting the 2,048-token limit.




                                                


Figure 5: Trainer-side AR evaluation: 128 test problems, one sampled answer each. This is a separate evaluation from the 500-problem greedy checkpoint sweep below.

title: Does RL in autoregressive decoding move the benchmark needle in diffusion decoding?
text:
Results




                                                


Figure 6: MATH Level 5, 500 test problems, greedy, one answer per problem. Step 0 is the base model. Error bars are ±1 standard error (about ±2.2 points). AR in vLLM, diffusion in SGLang (FastDiffuser, block 32, threshold 0.9).




And… it moves. Diffusion goes from 51.8% to between 55.2% and 59.0%, depending on the checkpoint. AR goes from 59.2% to between 63.0% and 66.8%.
Across the six checkpoints, AR gains 5.6 points on average and diffusion gains 5.3. Almost the same gain, even though diffusion never saw a masked block during training.
I also checked which of the 500 problems each checkpoint fixed or broke compared with step 0, using a McNemar test. For diffusion, the change from step 0 is significant at p < 0.05 at steps 25, 75, 125 and 150 (p = 0.007, 0.014, 0.002, 0.031). At steps 50 and 100 it isn’t (p = 0.09 and 0.16). AR is significant at every checkpoint except step 75 (p = 0.08). Those are unadjusted p-values across six checkpoint comparisons per mode. These checkpoints share a training run and test questions, so they aren’t independent experiments.
The gap doesn’t close, though. Diffusion is 7.4 points behind AR at step 0 and 8.0 behind at step 150.

GSM8K




                                                


Figure 7: GSM8K, 200 test questions, greedy, one answer per problem. Step 0 is the base model. Error bars are ±1 standard error (about ±2.3 points). None of the changes from step 0 is significant at p < 0.05 (McNemar, per mode).




On GSM8K, AR goes from 87.5% to between 88.0% and 91.5%, and diffusion from 86.5% to between 87.0% and 89.5%. None of the changes from step 0 is statistically significant. I don’t see a clear regression here, but 200 questions can’t rule out smaller changes or tell me what happens on other tasks.

title: Does RL in autoregressive decoding move the benchmark needle in diffusion decoding?
text:
Running out of tokens
The longer answers run into the token limit at eval time too.
At step 0, 26 AR answers and 22 diffusion answers ran out of room. From step 50 on it’s between 93 and 138 in each mode, so a fifth to a quarter of all answers get cut off before they reach a \boxed{}. I looked at the cut-off diffusion answers from step 75, and they aren’t loops, they’re just long, careful markdown solutions that run out of tokens.
RL is partly fighting its own length here: TRL drops truncated completions from the loss.
I also caught a mismatch while writing this: the AR eval in vLLM had a 2,048-token context, so the answer budget was 2,048 minus the prompt (45 to 1,087 tokens). Diffusion got 2,048 new tokens. Longer answers after training mean that mismatch can affect the measured gains too. I’ve fixed the budget setup for the next run.
I’d like to try this with a bigger answer budget and more seeds. This was one run of one 3B model, and I used the test split to pick a difficulty level and monitor training. Next time, those decisions need a separate set.







Eval settings





For the first diffusion numbers I used NVIDIA’s HF generate() with block size 32 and confidence threshold 0.9, which is what the model card shows. It works, but it decodes one problem at a time. On 300 Level-5 problems it ran at about 77 tokens/s per GPU. At that rate, evaluating 7 checkpoints × 700 problems would take too long.
At the time of this run, the vLLM diffusion path I looked at supported DiffusionGemma, and each model brought its own sampler, so using this model there would have needed a port. NVIDIA’s own serving code is an SGLang PR, sgl-project/sglang#25803, which adds this model with FastDiffuser (plain diffusion mode) plus CUDA graphs and batching. I built that branch in its own environment, since it wants torch 2.11, with the same settings as the HF run: 32-token blocks, threshold 0.9, a causal pass to seed each block.
Getting it to start on this box took three fixes, all on the environment side. There’s no CUDA toolkit on the node, so I pointed CUDA_HOME at the one that ships in the venv. FlashInfer tried to compile its kernels and failed, so I installed its prebuilt kernels the same way the PR’s Dockerfile does. And pip had pulled a CUDA 13.4 compiler next to a 13.0 runtime, so I pinned the compiler packages back to 13.0.
After that: about 1,340 tokens/s per GPU. 300 problems in 97 seconds.
But the accuracy didn’t match. On the same 300 problems SGLang got 52.3%, HF got 56.3%. Only 27 of the 300 answers were word for word the same, and the rest split after about 400 characters (the median), which is consistent with greedy decoding diverging after small numerical differences between engines. I did not isolate the cause. On the problems where they disagree, HF alone was right on 32 and SGLang alone on 20. That’s a McNemar p of about 0.10, so the gap could be noise, but I can’t call it zero either. So the rule from here on: every checkpoint goes through SGLang, and I only compare SGLang numbers with SGLang numbers.

Building Production Ready Text-to-SQL Agent from Scratch
text:
am.
  
    Writing
    Work
    Projects
    Talks
Let me be honest… I don’t like writing SQL queries. And I always wished if someone could do it for me. Well that’s exactly what we are going to do today!
We are going to build an intelligent agent that does just that, using Google’s Gemini model and creating a neat web interface with Gradio.
Traditional Text-to-SQL pipelines can sometimes be a bit like a black box. You give them a question, they spit out a SQL query, and you hope for the best.
What’s the advantage of building something more “agent-like,” even in a simplified form?
A standard text-to-sql pipeline can be brittle. The generated SQL query might be incorrect. Even worse, an incorrect query could run without errors but give you wrong or useless results, and you might not even realize it!
👉 While a full-fledged agent system might involve complex reasoning and self-correction, our approach today focuses on building a robust pipeline with clear steps, good error handling when talking to the Large Language Model (LLM), and a way to learn from the process. This lays the foundation for more advanced agentic behavior later.
Let’s build this agent! 💪
And by the way, all the code related to this guide can be found here on my github.

title: Building Production Ready Text-to-SQL Agent from Scratch
section: The Big Picture: Our Agent’s Workflow
text:
The Big Picture: Our Agent’s Workflow
Before we dive into code, let’s look at the overall flow of our system. It’s a simple, logical sequence: a user’s question comes in one end, and an answer from the database comes out the other.

title: Building Production Ready Text-to-SQL Agent from Scratch
text:
Setting the Stage - Our Database
First things first, every SQL agent needs a database to talk to! For this tutorial, we’ll use SQLite, which is super convenient because it’s a file-based database and doesn’t require a separate server.
Our Data: We’ll imagine a simple company database with two main tables:

departments: Stores information about different departments.
employees: Stores information about employees and which department they belong to.

Here’s the structure (schema) we’ll aim for:

This setup allows us to ask interesting questions like “Which employees work in Engineering?” or “What’s the average salary in the HR department?”.
To bring this to life, we need a script to create and populate this database. This ensures our agent always has a consistent environment to work in.
For those who want to see exactly how the database is created, you can check out the database_setup.py file in the GitHub repo. It’s a straightforward Python script using the sqlite3 library.
This script, when called by our UI application, will ensure we always have a fresh database with this structure and data for our agent to work with.

title: Building Production Ready Text-to-SQL Agent from Scratch
Building Production Ready Text-to-SQL Agent from Scratch
section: The Core Logic of our Text2SQL Agent
text:
The Core Logic of our Text2SQL Agent
Our agent’s job can be broken down into a few key steps. Let’s look at the concepts behind the main methods.

Getting the Database Schema For an LLM to generate correct SQL, it must know the structure of your database. We need a method, let’s call it _get_database_schema, that connects to our SQLite file and programmatically extracts all table names, column names, and their data types. This schema is then passed to the LLM as part of the context.
Generating the SQL Query This is the heart of the agent, where we talk to Gemini. The process is called prompt engineering. We need to write a very clear set of instructions (a “prompt”) for the model.

Our prompt includes:

The Role: “You are an expert SQLite SQL query generator.”
The Context: The full database schema we just extracted.
The Task: The user’s question.
The Constraints: “Output ONLY the SQL query. No extra text or markdown.”

We then wrap this prompt and send it to the Gemini API using Google’s Python SDK.
# A conceptual look at the prompt structure inside the _generate_sql_with_gemini method

system_instruction_text = "You are an expert SQLite SQL query generator."

prompt_for_task = f"""
Database Schema:
---
{self.schema} 
---
Task: ...
Constraints: ...

User Question: {question}

SQL Query:
"""
full_prompt_for_gemini = f"{system_instruction_text}\n\n{prompt_for_task}"
response = self.gemini_model.generate_content(full_prompt_for_gemini, ...)
Full code can be found here.

Executing the Query Once Gemini returns what we hope is a valid SQL query, our agent needs to run it. A method _execute_sql_query connects to the database, executes the string, and fetches the results.

A quick note on security: In a real-world application, directly running LLM-generated SQL can be risky. For this educational project, we’re keeping it simple, but in production, you would add validation layers or use read-only database permissions.
Our Adventure with Gemini: From Bugs to Best Practices
Working with powerful LLMs is an iterative process. It’s rarely perfect on the first try! Here are some real challenges we faced and the key lessons learned.
Best Practices We Adopted:

Clear, Instructive Prompts: Be explicit about the role, context, task, and constraints.
Configuration for Determinism: Using temperature=0.0 for SQL generation tells the model to be predictable and factual, not creative.
Handling API Responses Carefully: Never assume the LLM’s response will be perfect. Always check for errors, finish_reason, and empty content before processing the output.

Bugs Along the Way (and How We Squashed Them!):

The “Empty Schema” Mystery: At first, our agent wasn’t sending the schema! Gemini received an empty prompt and couldn’t work. By meticulously printing the exact prompt string before sending it, we found the bug in our schema-loading logic and fixed it.
The MAX_TOKENS Puzzle: Even with the schema, our first model (a preview version) would often fail with finish_reason: MAX_TOKENS and no output. It seemed to be getting confused by the long, complex prompt.


The “Aha!” Moment: We used the “Extreme Prompt Simplification Test” we replaced our complex prompt with a simple question like “What is the capital of France?”. When that worked, it proved our API setup was fine and the issue was with how that specific model handled our complex prompt.
The Fix: Increasing max_output_tokens resolved this!


The response.text Trap: Using response.text to get the output can fail if the model’s response is blocked or empty. We learned to robustly parse response.candidates[0].content.parts instead.

Key Takeaway: Debugging LLM interactions is an art. Log your inputs (prompts) and its outputs (raw responses) very carefully!

section: Bringing Our Agent to Life with Gradio
text:
Bringing Our Agent to Life with Gradio
Now, let’s build a cool UI! We want a chat window with clickable question suggestions on the side. For this custom layout, we’ll use Gradio’s gr.Blocks().
(Here you could insert a screenshot of the final Gradio UI)
The UI has three main parts:

The Chatbot Display: A gr.Chatbot component shows the history of the conversation.
The Suggestion Column: We create a gr.Column and loop through a list of example questions, creating a gr.Button for each. The magic happens in the .click() event handler for each button, which updates the main input box.
The Input Area: A gr.Textbox for typing messages and a “Send” gr.Button. Both are wired to a single function, handle_chat_submission, which orchestrates the interaction with our agent.

This function takes the user’s message and the chat history, passes them to our agent’s .run() method, gets the result, and updates the chat display.
For the specific code that wires up these Gradio components, feel free to check out ui/app_text2sql.py in the repository.

title: Building Production Ready Text-to-SQL Agent from Scratch
section: How Good is Our Agent? A Note on Evaluation
text:
How Good is Our Agent? A Note on Evaluation
Creating an agent is just the first step. To know if it’s truly useful, especially for production, we need to evaluate it.
Key Evaluation Metrics for Text-to-SQL:

Execution Accuracy: This is the most important one. Does the generated SQL run without errors and produce the correct answer? You’d need a test dataset of questions and their known correct answers to verify this.
Query Match: Does the generated SQL query exactly match a “golden” or reference SQL query? This is very strict and often not necessary, as multiple different SQL queries can produce the same correct result.
Robustness: How well does the agent handle ambiguous questions, questions about things not in the schema, or slightly malformed inputs?

For a real project, you would build a “test suite” of many question-query-answer triplets and run your agent against it to calculate these metrics automatically. This helps track improvements as you refine your prompts or change models.

title: Building Production Ready Text-to-SQL Agent from Scratch
text:
Conclusion
And there you have it! We’ve journeyed from understanding the need for a robust Text-to-SQL solution, setting up our database, architecting a scalable agent structure, and diving deep into the logic using Gemini. We navigated some tricky debugging and wrapped it all in a user-friendly Gradio interface.
You’ve now built a functional Text-to-SQL agent from scratch! This project covers many important concepts: OOP, database interaction, LLM prompting, debugging, and web UI creation.
This project touches on many important concepts:

Object-Oriented Programming (base classes, inheritance)
Database Interaction (SQLite)
LLM Prompt Engineering and API Usage (Gemini)
Debugging and Iterative Development
Web UI Creation (Gradio)

Feel free to experiment further:

Make the agent use conversation history for follow-up questions.
Add more error handling or self-correction attempts if the SQL fails.
Try different LLMs or prompting strategies.
Expand the Gradio UI with more features!

Happy coding, and keep building amazing things!

title: Making GEMV Fast
text:
